claim: Categorical sensory representations are critical for many behaviors, including speech perception.
source: Categorical sensory representations are critical for many behaviors, including speech perception.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of sensory neuroscience.

claim: In the auditory system, categorical information is thought to arise hierarchically, becoming increasingly prominent in higher-order cortical regions.
source: In the auditory system, categorical information is thought to arise hierarchically, becoming increasingly prominent in higher-order cortical regions.
evidence: This represents established theoretical understanding in auditory neuroscience.

claim: Task engagement caused categorical sound representations to emerge in non-primary auditory cortex.
source: Population-level decoding of simultaneously recorded single neurons revealed that task engagement caused categorical sound representations to emerge in non-primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from population decoding analysis.

claim: In primary auditory cortex, task engagement caused a general enhancement of sound decoding that was not specific to task-relevant categories.
source: In primary auditory cortex, task engagement caused a general enhancement of sound decoding that was not specific to task-relevant categories.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from A1 recordings.

claim: These findings are consistent with mixed selectivity models of neural disentanglement.
source: These findings are consistent with mixed selectivity models of neural disentanglement, in which early sensory regions build an overcomplete representation of the world and allow neurons in downstream brain regions to flexibly and selectively read out behaviorally relevant, categorical information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models.

claim: During language processing, vowels are perceived categorically, even though the formant frequencies that define them vary continuously across utterances.
source: For example, during language processing, vowels are perceived categorically, even though the formant frequencies that define them vary continuously across utterances (Hillenbrand et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Subjects can learn to classify arbitrary, novel sounds according to one spectro-temporal feature while ignoring others.
source: Categorical perception is not limited to language, as subjects can learn to classify arbitrary, novel sounds according to one spectro-temporal feature while ignoring others (Stilp and Kluender, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Engaging in auditory behavior can enhance sensory discriminability at the level of single neurons.
source: Neurophysiological studies in auditory cortex have shown that engaging in auditory behavior can enhance sensory discriminability at the level of single neurons (Buran et al., 2014; Niwa et al., 2012a) and neural populations (Bagur et al., 2018; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Engaging in auditory behavior can enhance sensory discriminability at the level of neural populations.
source: Neurophysiological studies in auditory cortex have shown that engaging in auditory behavior can enhance sensory discriminability at the level of single neurons (Buran et al., 2014; Niwa et al., 2012a) and neural populations (Bagur et al., 2018; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In frontal cortex, neurons often only encode sound categories.
source: In frontal cortex, neurons often only encode sound categories (Fritz et al., 2010; Tsunada et al., 2011), suggesting that sound information is transformed into an invariant, categorical representation before exiting auditory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sound information is transformed into an invariant, categorical representation before exiting auditory cortex.
source: In frontal cortex, neurons often only encode sound categories (Fritz et al., 2010; Tsunada et al., 2011), suggesting that sound information is transformed into an invariant, categorical representation before exiting auditory cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited observations in frontal cortex.

claim: Neural systems can produce invariant representations through hierarchical computation with mixed selectivity in early processing regions.
source: Theory predicts that neural systems can produce these invariant representations through hierarchical computation. In early processing regions, mixed selectivity of single neurons produces high-dimensional, overcomplete representations of sensory inputs and behavioral variables. From this population activity, it is straightforward for neurons in downstream areas to decode information about a specific feature that is important to the current behavior and whose representation is invariant to irrelevant sensory information (Kell et al., 2018; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The effects of task engagement are larger in non-primary auditory fields.
source: Previous work has shown that the effects of task engagement are larger in non-primary auditory fields (Atiani et al., 2014; Kline et al., 2023; Niwa et al., 2013), as are the effects of selective attention, which may be related to invariant sound feature coding (O'Sullivan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Choice-related activity emerges in non-primary auditory cortex during a challenging perceptual discrimination behavior.
source: Some studies have also reported that choice-related activity emerges in non-primary auditory cortex during a challenging perceptual discrimination behavior (Tsunada et al., 2016), although factors affecting choice coding may be task-dependent (Bizley et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Behaviorally relevant neural representations are computed hierarchically in auditory cortex.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with the idea that behaviorally relevant neural representations are computed hierarchically in auditory cortex (Lestang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior work.

claim: Four male ferrets were trained to perform a go/no-go tone-in-noise detection task.
source: To study how neural representations of sound category emerge in auditory cortex, we trained four male ferrets to perform a go/no-go tone-in-noise detection task.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and subjects used in the study.

claim: Animals reported the occurrence of a target tone by licking a piezo spout.
source: Animals reported the occurrence of a target tone in a sequence of narrowband noise distractors by licking a piezo spout (Figure 1A, Methods: Behavioral paradigm, distractor stimulus sound level: 60 dB SPL).
evidence: This describes the behavioral response method used in the task.

claim: Behavioral performance showed a clear psychometric dependence on target SNR.
source: Across behavioral sessions and animals, performance showed a clear psychometric dependence on target SNR (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by behavioral data shown in the figures.

claim: All animals could easily discriminate between the pure tone (Inf dB) target and catch stimulus.
source: All animals could easily discriminate between the pure tone (Inf dB) target and catch stimulus, while performance for lower SNR target stimuli approached the chance level.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral performance data.

claim: Performance for lower SNR target stimuli approached the chance level.
source: All animals could easily discriminate between the pure tone (Inf dB) target and catch stimulus, while performance for lower SNR target stimuli approached the chance level.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral performance data.

claim: Linear 64-channel silicon probes were used to record single-unit activity from primary (A1) and non-primary (dPEG) auditory cortex.
source: We used linear 64-channel silicon probes (Shobe et al., 2015) to record single-unit activity from primary (A1) and non-primary (dPEG) auditory cortex while animals performed the tone-in-noise detection task.
evidence: This describes the recording methodology used in the study.

claim: Recordings were targeted to each respective region based on functional mapping of neural responses.
source: Recordings were targeted to each respective region based on functional mapping of neural responses (Methods, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the targeting methodology for recordings.

claim: Behavior alternated between blocks of active task engagement and passive listening to task stimuli.
source: Behavior alternated between blocks of active task engagement and passive listening to task stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During passive listening, licking responses were not rewarded and animals quickly disengaged from the task.
source: During passive listening, licking responses were not rewarded and animals quickly disengaged from the task (David et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the passive listening condition, with a citation to prior work.

claim: In both A1 and dPEG, responses to target and catch stimuli were significantly discriminable for about 25% of single neurons.
source: In both A1 and dPEG, responses to target and catch stimuli were significantly discriminable for a subset of single neurons (about 25% in both areas, Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4, bootstrap test).
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron analysis.

claim: Task engagement was associated with significant changes in catch vs. target d-prime for roughly 10% of neurons in both A1 and dPEG.
source: Task engagement was associated with significant changes in catch vs. target d-prime for roughly 10% of neurons in both A1 (40/481 neurons, bootstrap test) and dPEG (33/377 neurons, bootstrap test).
evidence: This is a finding from the single neuron analysis.

claim: The effects of task engagement at the level of single neurons were relatively mild and inconsistent across the population.
source: Thus, the effects of task engagement at the level of single neurons were relatively mild and inconsistent across the population; many neurons showed no significant change, and of those that did, the effects were bidirectional (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single neuron data.

claim: In both A1 and dPEG, population d-prime for catch versus target stimuli consistently increased during task engagement.
source: In both A1 and dPEG, population d-prime for catch versus target stimuli consistently increased during task engagement.
evidence: This is a finding from the population decoding analysis.

claim: In A1, the increase in d-prime was consistent across all task categories with no difference between target vs. target and target vs. catch discrimination accuracy.
source: In A1, the increase in d-prime was consistent across all task categories; there was no difference between target vs. target and target vs. catch discrimination accuracy (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the population decoding analysis in A1.

claim: In dPEG, the improvement of task-relevant catch vs. target discrimination was significantly larger than in any other category.
source: However, in dPEG the improvement of task-relevant catch vs. target discrimination was significantly larger than in any other category (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the population decoding analysis in dPEG.

claim: Discrimination of task-relevant sound categories was selectively enhanced in non-primary auditory cortex.
source: Unlike A1, discrimination of task-relevant sound categories was selectively enhanced in non-primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the population decoding analysis.

claim: Task engagement is often correlated with increased arousal.
source: Importantly, task engagement is often correlated with increased arousal (de Gee et al., 2022; Saderi et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in the supplement.

claim: Decoding analysis was performed after first removing all spiking variability that could be explained using pupil-indexed arousal.
source: To ensure that our results were not influenced by non-specific effects of arousal, decoding analysis was performed after first removing all spiking variability that could be explained using pupil-indexed arousal (Methods).
evidence: This describes a methodological control used in the analysis.

claim: Performing the same decoding analysis without first controlling for pupil size did not affect the selective enhancement observed in dPEG.
source: Performing the same decoding analysis without first controlling for pupil size did not affect the selective enhancement that we observed in dPEG (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis.

claim: Pupil-indexed arousal primarily operates on an orthogonal subspace to the global task engagement axis and tends to non-specifically improve coding accuracy.
source: The absence of a pupil effect on selectivity suggests that pupil-indexed arousal primarily operates on an orthogonal subspace to the global task engagement axis and tends to non-specifically improve coding accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the control analysis results.

claim: Across animals, task stimuli evoked robust pupil dilation that varied with the trial outcome.
source: Across animals, task stimuli evoked robust pupil dilation that varied with the trial outcome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupil analysis.

claim: Pre-trial pupil size was significantly different between correct (hit and correct reject), hit, and miss trials.
source: Notably, pre-trial pupil size was significantly different between correct (hit and correct reject), hit, and miss trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–c), recapitulating the finding of an inverted-U relationship to performance in rodents (McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the pupil analysis, with a citation to prior work.

claim: A significant correlation was found between neural d-prime and behavioral d-prime for populations in dPEG, but not in A1.
source: We found a significant correlation for populations in dPEG, but not in A1 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The task-specific changes in dPEG are coupled with the behavioral output reflecting those sound features.
source: Thus, the task-specific changes in dPEG are coupled with the behavioral output reflecting those sound features.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between neural and behavioral d-prime.

claim: In both brain regions choice could be decoded well above chance level.
source: We found that in both brain regions choice could be decoded well above chance level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the choice probability analysis.

claim: Choice information was present throughout the entire trial and did not increase during the target stimulus presentation.
source: Choice information was present throughout the entire trial and did not increase during the target stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a finding from the choice probability analysis.

claim: The difference in population activity primarily reflects a cognitive state associated with the probability of licking on a given trial, or 'impulsivity' rather than 'choice.'
source: This suggests that the difference in population activity primarily reflects a cognitive state associated with the probability of licking on a given trial, or 'impulsivity' rather than 'choice.'
evidence: This is an interpretation of the choice probability analysis results.

claim: Covariability patterns changed significantly between the passive and active states.
source: We found that covariability patterns changed significantly between the passive and active states (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the factor analysis.

claim: In both brain regions, task engagement caused a rotation of the principal covariability axis, consistent with an overall decorrelation of population activity.
source: In both brain regions, task engagement caused a rotation of the principal covariability axis, consistent with an overall decorrelation of population activity (Umakantha et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the factor analysis, with a citation to prior work.

claim: In A1, task engagement caused covariability to become more aligned with the sound discrimination axis.
source: Surprisingly, in A1, task engagement caused covariability to become more aligned with the sound discrimination axis.
evidence: This is a finding from the alignment analysis.

claim: In dPEG alignment was low in both the passive and engaged states.
source: Conversely, in dPEG alignment was low in both the passive and engaged states, consistent with covariability reflecting non-sensory variables that do not directly interact with the processing of the sensory stimulus (Stringer et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a finding from the alignment analysis, with a citation to prior work.

claim: A simulation in which population covariability was fixed and only the evoked response gain changed between passive and active conditions (gain only) was sufficient to produce task-relevant selectivity in non-primary auditory cortex.
source: A simulation in which population covariability was fixed and only the evoked response gain changed between passive and active conditions (gain only) was sufficient to produce task-relevant selectivity in non-primary auditory cortex (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: Task-dependent changes in evoked response gain, not population covariability, support the emergence of a behaviorally relevant population code in non-primary auditory cortex.
source: Thus, task-dependent changes in evoked response gain, not population covariability, support the emergence of a behaviorally relevant population code in non-primary auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation analysis.

claim: Gain modulation alone was sufficient to recapitulate the choice information present in the raw data for this task.
source: Similar to our findings for stimulus decoding, we found that gain modulation alone was sufficient to recapitulate the choice information present in the raw data for this task.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis of choice information.

claim: In A1, task engagement improved neural coding uniformly across all sound categories, both relevant and irrelevant to the current task.
source: In A1, task engagement improved neural coding uniformly across all sound categories, both relevant and irrelevant to the current task.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding in A1.

claim: In dPEG, the neural population selectively enhanced the representation only of sound categories relevant to the tone-in-noise behavior.
source: In dPEG, on the other hand, the neural population selectively enhanced the representation only of sound categories relevant to the tone-in-noise behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding in dPEG.

claim: Task-dependent changes in neural response gain were sufficient to account for emergent selectivity.
source: Task-dependent changes in neural response gain were sufficient to account for this emergent selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation analysis.

claim: The pattern of task-related effects is consistent with a hierarchical, mixed selectivity model of sensory decision-making.
source: The pattern of task-related effects is consistent with a hierarchical, mixed selectivity model of sensory decision-making (Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models, with a citation.

claim: Neural populations in early brain areas form a sparse, overcomplete representation of sensory inputs, which supports a simple linear readout of task-relevant features in downstream areas.
source: Neural populations in early brain areas form a sparse, overcomplete representation of sensory inputs, which supports a simple linear readout of task-relevant features in downstream areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models.

claim: Task-dependent modulation of auditory responses is larger in non-primary versus primary fields of auditory cortex.
source: Prior work has established that task-dependent modulation of auditory responses is larger in non-primary versus primary fields of auditory cortex (Atiani et al., 2014; Kline et al., 2023; Niwa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Behaviorally relevant representations first emerged in the non-primary field, dPEG.
source: We found a clear dissociation between cortical fields; behaviorally relevant representations first emerged in the non-primary field, dPEG.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: In the frontal cortex (FC) of ferrets engaged in a similar tone detection behavior, single-neuron activity is behaviorally gated.
source: In the frontal cortex (FC) of ferrets engaged in a similar tone detection behavior, single-neuron activity is behaviorally gated.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work in frontal cortex.

claim: Responses to a set of target tones are strongly enhanced when they require a behavioral response.
source: Responses to a set of target tones are strongly enhanced when they require a behavioral response (Fritz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: The enhanced category representation in dPEG supports a simple linear readout of 'go' versus 'no-go' categories that could provide input to category-specific neurons in FC.
source: In our task, the enhanced category representation in dPEG supports a simple linear readout of 'go' versus 'no-go' categories that could provide input to category-specific neurons in FC.
evidence: This is a speculation about how dPEG activity might relate to downstream processing.

claim: Decoding accuracy in dPEG tracked the animal's behavioral performance.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that the selective enhancement of category representation is causally related to behavior, we found that decoding accuracy in dPEG tracked the animal's behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Choice-related activity is present or is stronger in non-primary versus primary auditory cortex.
source: This correlation between neural activity and behavioral performance is consistent with previous observations that choice-related activity is present or is stronger in non-primary versus primary auditory cortex (Bizley et al., 2013; Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Some other studies have reported choice-related activity emerging as early as A1.
source: However, some other studies have reported choice-related activity emerging as early as A1 (Niwa et al., 2012b; Selezneva et al., 2006), suggesting that the role of different cortical regions in decision-making may depend on aspects of the task, including the specifics of the auditory stimuli and the associated motor response.
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Analysis of sound discriminability at the population level revealed striking qualitative differences between A1 and dPEG.
source: Despite the diverse task-dependent changes in sound representations across individual neurons, analysis of sound discriminability at the population level revealed striking qualitative differences between A1 and dPEG.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Population coding accuracy is defined as the amount of stimulus information an ideal observer could extract from simultaneously recorded population activity.
source: In our analysis, we defined population coding accuracy as the amount of stimulus information an ideal observer could extract from simultaneously recorded population activity.
evidence: This describes the definition used in the analysis.

claim: These measures do not necessarily reflect the information utilized by the animal.
source: Thus, our results should be interpreted as an upper bound on the information transmitted by a group of neurons about a particular stimulus. Critically, these measures do not necessarily reflect the information utilized by the animal.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the results.

claim: In A1, there was a decoding axis for every stimulus category along which task engagement improved sound representation.
source: In A1, for example, we found a decoding axis for every stimulus category along which task engagement improved sound representation.
evidence: This is a finding from the population decoding analysis.

claim: Despite this global improvement in A1, decoding downstream in dPEG was only improved for task-relevant sounds.
source: Despite this global improvement in A1, decoding downstream in dPEG was only improved for task-relevant sounds.
evidence: This is a finding from the population decoding analysis.

claim: During the engaged state, dPEG reads out activity along an axis of A1 population activity that is invariant to task-irrelevant stimuli.
source: This selective change indicates that dPEG does not always read out information optimally from A1. Instead, during the engaged state, it reads out activity along an axis of A1 population activity that is invariant to task-irrelevant stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The brain must first build overcomplete, high-dimensional representations of the sensory world.
source: Theories of neural disentanglement and the formation of categorical representations posit that the brain must first build overcomplete, high-dimensional representations of the sensory world (DiCarlo and Cox, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical models, supported by a citation.

claim: From this high-dimensional activity, it is straightforward to build a linear decoder, tuned to the task at hand, that extracts only task-relevant information.
source: From this high-dimensional activity, it is straightforward to build a linear decoder, tuned to the task at hand, that extracts only task-relevant information (Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical models, supported by a citation.

claim: The findings describe a hierarchical network for computing sound categories.
source: Our findings are consistent with this theory and describe a hierarchical network for computing sound categories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of theoretical models.

claim: An overcomplete representation in A1 is selectively filtered at the population level in dPEG.
source: An overcomplete representation in A1 is selectively filtered at the population level in dPEG, and subsequently, this activity may provide input to category-specific neurons in areas such as FC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Simultaneously recording the activity of populations of neurons allowed investigation of how trial-by-trial covariability across the population depends on task engagement and contributes to sound encoding.
source: This approach allowed us to investigate how trial-by-trial covariability across the population depends on task engagement and contributes to sound encoding.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the experimental approach.

claim: Trial-by-trial covariance can impair population coding accuracy.
source: Theoretical work has shown that trial-by-trial covariance can impair population coding accuracy (Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical work, supported by a citation.

claim: Early experiments in visual cortex demonstrated that selective attention improves perceptual discriminations primarily by reducing covariance.
source: Early experiments in visual cortex supported this idea, demonstrating that selective attention improves perceptual discriminations primarily by reducing covariance (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Task engagement modulated covariability patterns in both A1 and dPEG.
source: We found task engagement modulated covariability patterns in both A1 and dPEG, broadly consistent with prior work in the auditory system (Downer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the factor analysis, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The changes in covariance had no impact on emergent behavioral selectivity in dPEG or on the mean generalized improvement in sound coding in A1.
source: Strikingly, however, the changes in covariance had no impact on emergent behavioral selectivity in dPEG or on the mean generalized improvement in sound coding in A1.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulation analysis.

claim: In A1, covariability became more aligned with the behaviorally relevant sensory decoding axis during task engagement.
source: In A1, we found that covariability became more aligned with the behaviorally relevant sensory decoding axis during task engagement.
evidence: This is a finding from the alignment analysis.

claim: Covariability in A1 primarily reflects top-down gain modulation that drives changes in selectivity.
source: Instead, we hypothesize that covariability in A1 primarily reflects top-down gain modulation that drives changes in selectivity (Denfield et al., 2018; Goris et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings, with citations to prior work.

claim: During the task-engaged state, top-down signals selectively modulate sound-evoked responses of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli.
source: During the task-engaged state, top-down signals selectively modulate sound-evoked responses of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli, thus boosting the representation of task-relevant sounds for downstream readout.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: If gain is not perfectly static, but varies in strength from trial to trial, this could explain the observed increase in covariability amongst task-relevant neurons.
source: If gain is not perfectly static, but varies in strength from trial to trial, this could explain the observed increase in covariability amongst task-relevant neurons (Denfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The direction of covariability in dPEG changed randomly with respect to the behaviorally relevant decoding axis.
source: In contrast, the direction of covariability in dPEG changed randomly with respect to the behaviorally relevant decoding axis.
evidence: This is a finding from the alignment analysis.

claim: During both passive and engaged states, covariability remained mostly orthogonal to the sensory decoding axis and, therefore, had little impact on population decoding accuracy.
source: During both passive and engaged states, covariability remained mostly orthogonal to the sensory decoding axis and, therefore, had little impact on population decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a finding from the alignment analysis.

claim: Trial-by-trial covariability is primarily orthogonal to sensory coding dimensions and reflects non-sensory motor or cognitive variables, such as whisking, running, or arousal.
source: These findings are consistent with recent work suggesting that trial-by-trial covariability is primarily orthogonal to sensory coding dimensions and reflects non-sensory motor or cognitive variables, such as whisking, running, or arousal (Musall et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work, with citations.

claim: Covariability does not usually reflect information limiting noise, but instead reflects important cognitive processes active in different brain regions during sensory decision-making.
source: Our results contribute to a growing body of evidence that covariability does not usually reflect information limiting noise, but instead reflects important cognitive processes active in different brain regions during sensory decision-making (Srinath et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior work, with a citation.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Oregon Health and Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC protocol IP1561).
source: All procedures were approved by the Oregon Health and Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC protocol IP1561) and conform to the standard of the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care (AAALAC).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Adult male domestic ferrets were acquired from an animal supplier (Marshall BioResources).
source: Adult male domestic ferrets were acquired from an animal supplier (Marshall BioResources).
evidence: This describes the source of the experimental subjects.

claim: Two stainless steel head-posts were fixed to the skull along the midline with bone cement (Palacos or Charisma).
source: Two stainless steel head-posts were fixed to the skull along the midline with bone cement (Palacos or Charisma).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: Recording sites were targeted based on external landmarks and tonotopic maps.
source: Recording sites were targeted based on external landmarks and tonotopic maps (Atiani et al., 2014; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the targeting methodology, with citations to prior work.

claim: Licks occurring during a target window (0.2–1.0 s following target onset) were rewarded with a high-protein, high-calorie supplement (Ensure).
source: Licks occurring during a target window (0.2–1.0 s following target onset) were rewarded with a high-protein, high-calorie supplement (Ensure), while licks outside the window were penalized with a timeout (3–10 s).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: The number of distractor stimuli per trial was distributed randomly with a flat hazard function to prevent behavioral timing strategies.
source: The number of distractor stimuli per trial was distributed randomly with a flat hazard function to prevent behavioral timing strategies.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: Electrode contacts were spaced 20 μm horizontally and 25 μm vertically in three columns, collectively spanning 1.05 mm of cortex.
source: Electrode contacts were spaced 20 μm horizontally and 25 μm vertically in three columns, collectively spanning 1.05 mm of cortex.
evidence: This describes the recording electrode configuration.

claim: Spike sorting was performed using Kilosort2.
source: Spike sorting was performed using Kilosort2 (Pachitariu et al., 2016), followed by curation in phy (https://github.com/cortex-lab/phy; Rossant, 2024).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting methodology, with citations.

claim: Neurons were confirmed to be in A1 based on stereotypical response properties: short latency responses to sound onset, sharp and consistent frequency tuning across layers, and a characteristic dorsal-ventral tonotopic map across penetrations.
source: Neurons were confirmed to be in A1 based on stereotypical response properties: short latency responses to sound onset, sharp and consistent frequency tuning across layers, and a characteristic dorsal-ventral tonotopic map across penetrations (Shamma et al., 1993).
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying A1, with a citation to prior work.

claim: The border between A1 and dPEG was defined as the location where the tonotopic map gradient reversed.
source: Once A1 was located, subsequent craniotomies were opened in small lateral steps. Tuning was measured at each recording site, and the border between A1 and dPEG was defined as the location where the tonotopic map gradient reversed (Atiani et al., 2014; Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying the border between A1 and dPEG, with citations to prior work.

claim: Pupil size was shifted 750ms relative to spike times in order to account for the previously reported lagged relationship between neural activity and pupil in cortex.
source: Pupil size was shifted 750ms relative to spike times in order to account for the previously reported lagged relationship between neural activity and pupil in cortex (McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the pupil analysis methodology, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Behavioral performance was measured using d-prime, defined as the z-scored difference between the target hit rate and false alarm rate across a behavior session.
source: Behavioral performance was measured using d-prime (Green and Swets, 1966), defined as the z-scored difference between the target hit rate and false alarm rate across a behavior session.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance metric, with a citation.

claim: A d-prime of 0 indicates chance level performance.
source: A d-prime of 0 indicates chance level performance.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the d-prime metric.

claim: To avoid overfitting, dDR was performed prior to computing the discrimination axis.
source: To avoid overfitting, we performed dDR prior to computing the discrimination axis (Heller and David, 2022).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to avoid overfitting, with a citation.

claim: Factor analysis is the simplest form of dimensionality reduction that explicitly separates shared variance across neurons from independent variance of single neurons.
source: Factor analysis is the simplest form of dimensionality reduction that explicitly separates shared variance across neurons from independent variance of single neurons, decomposing the spike count covariance matrix into two parts, a covariance matrix representing shared variance between neurons (Σshared) and a diagonal matrix representing the independent variance of each single neuron (Ψ):
evidence: This describes the factor analysis methodology.
